title: Agency Is the Oxygen of Learning
author: Shari Keller
summary: Shari Keller argues that when children lose ownership of micro-decisions in learning tasks, they stop thinking and merely comply with instructions. Kids need to try before asking, reread confusing passages, guess answers, and test ideas themselves for learning to feel meaningful and intentional. Well-meaning parents who jump in quickly to prevent struggle inadvertently teach deference over thinking, producing students who disconnect work from meaning and stop attempting when confident in their capacity. This learned helplessness creates adults who must relearn trying, testing ideas, and trusting their thinking after years of deference to authority figures. Restoring ownership requires coaching with questions, strategic pause, and genuine belief that the child can try first before borrowing the parent's thought.
points: Kids care about work they take part in, not work they simply carry out; losing agency in learning transforms schoolwork into a task to finish rather than thinking to do.
When children lack role in their own learning, willingness to bring ideas drops to almost zero as they believe their thinking doesn't change anything.
Well-meaning parents taught to prevent struggle and keep things moving accidentally disconnect children from the mental friction required for learning and retention.
Kids who grow up with lost agency often become adults who must relearn trying, testing ideas, and trusting their thinking after years of deference to authority.
Restoring ownership requires coaching with questions, pause, and belief that the child can try first before borrowing the parent's thought.
quotes: Kids care most about the work they take part in, not the work they just carry out. When your kid has no role in their own learning, they don't have a role in thinking.
When kids lose ownership of the micro decisions inside thinking, nothing dramatic happens. But your kid stops thinking for themselves. They're finishing a task, not working with it.

The safest approach becomes something like: Just tell me what you want, and I'll do that. Sure it might produce a good student who gets good grades but your kid's willingness to bring their own ideas usually drops off.

Kids don't really learn just by carrying out instructions. They learn when they think. All those micro moments when your kid tries first, even before they fully understand, is the oxygen that fuels learning.

Restoring ownership doesn't mean pulling away. It means inviting your kid back into the thinking in small ways, consistently and with compassion, as a coach who believes your kid can do it.” Archived from Quest for Learning on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
